Good evening, everyone, and welcome to the special council meeting on January 26, 2026.
Individuals interested in participating in this evening's meeting were eligible to register
online using the delegation registration form at www.kitchener.ca slash delegation or via email
at delegation at kitchener.ca. Any written comments received prior to the commencement of
today's meeting have been shared with members of Council and will form part of the public record.
The meeting live stream and archive videos are available at www.kitchener.ca slash watch now.
Before we begin this evening's meeting, I'd like to acknowledge that today we're gathering
on the traditional territory of the neutral Anishinaabe and Odena Shoni peoples.
We recognize our responsibility to serve as stewards for the land and honor their original
caretakers who came before us.
Our community is enriched by the enduring knowledge and deep rooted traditions of the
diverse First Nations, Métis, and Inuit in Kitchener today.
Before we begin today's special council meeting, I'd like to take a few moments to acknowledge
and paused to recognize the National Day of Remembrance of the Quebec City Mosque attack
and action against Islamophobia. On January 29, 2017, six lives were taken away in an act of terror.
We remember Ibrahima Berry, Mamadou Tanu Berry, Khaled Belkachemi, Abdelkarim Hassani,
Azadine Sufiani and Abu Bakr Tabti, men who were murdered while worshipping at the Centre
Culturel Islamique de Québec. This was an attack on the fundamental values of safety,
dignity, and freedom of worship. It was a painful reminder that Islamophobia is real,
it causes deep harm, has devastating consequences, and that we all share a responsibility to confront
it wherever it appears. I also want to acknowledge that January 27th marks the International
Holocaust Remembrance Day. On this day, we honour the 6 million Jews who were murdered during the
Holocaust, along with the countless others who were persecuted. As we reflect in one of the
darkest chapters in human history, we support survivors and their families and reaffirm our
shared responsibility to reflect on the dangers of anti-Semitism.
Education, remembrance, and unity remain our strongest tools as we continue building a
community rooted in dignity, kindness, compassion, and humanity.
Together, these commemorations remind us that hatred in any form threatens the safety and
well-being of our communities.
We stand firmly against hatred in all acts of terror.
No one should ever fear for their safety because of their faith or identity.
Every community deserves to live in peace, dignity, and security.
Today and every day, we must identify and address discrimination, support those affected by it,
and work together to build a Kitchener and a world where everyone belongs.
It takes each of us to choose to act with both intention and courage.
We must continue to foster a city, a country and a world that is inclusive, respectful and grounded in kindness and compassion.
As we reflect on these solid days of remembrance, it's equally important that we take meaningful actions in support of the affected communities.
One of those ways is by doing what we're all doing this evening, and that's participating in the National Council of Canadian Muslims Green Square campaign.
The green square represents the green carpets of the Centre Coulteral Islamique de Québec,
on which the victims last knelt in prayer.
It symbolizes the hope that the deceased are now at peace in a green garden.
In the days leading up to January 29,
please continue wearing the green square in memory of the victims
and in solidarity with the survivors, their families and friends,
and Muslim communities across Canada.
This campaign is a call to action for all Canadians
to stand together for a society free of hatred of all kinds,
and particularly in relation to Islamophobia,
not just today, but every day.
